title: The swan on the wheel
hookLine: a swan circles the wheel of lives, lost while it thinks it stands apart from God, until grace brings it home
carry: the soul wanders while it feels apart from god
last: NATURE TURNS THE WHEEL. GOD HOLDS THE HUB.

cards: Some weeks feel like flying in circles: the same rooms, the same worries, never quite landing, and somehow alone in it. The Shvetashvatara has a bird for that feeling.
A white bird, flying around and around, never coming down. And not on a tree this time, like the Mundaka's two birds you met six days ago. On the wheel.

teach.b: Verse 1.6, in paraphrase: in this huge wheel of Brahman, which lives in everything and holds everything, the swan wanders around and around, as long as it thinks that itself and the one who moves it are two different things.
When it is blessed by that one, it reaches what does not die. The word is hamsa, swan or wild goose.
In Hindu teaching the hamsa became a picture of the soul, the jiva: a bird that flies high and, tradition says, rests on water without getting wet. Put it inside yesterday's wheel.
It flies spoke to spoke, life to life, and never lands.
That circling has a name: samsara, the round of births. Here's the teaching, plainly. In Hinduism the soul's trouble isn't that it's bad.
It's that it feels apart: I'm out here on the rim, and the one who turns all this is somewhere else.
In chapter four this same Upanishad retells the two birds: the eating bird grieves until it sees the other, the Lord, and its grief falls away. The lost bird isn't fixed by flying harder.
It's freed by seeing who has been there all along.

And one word is new: blessed. The swan doesn't just figure it out; it is helped home. Advaita teachers read that as the self recognizing it was never separate; devotional schools, as a soul brought close by a loving Lord.
It's why some great renunciates carry the title Paramahamsa, the highest swan.

how: The hamsa appears as an image of the soul in Hindu songs and teaching, and Paramahamsa, 'highest swan', is a title given to some renunciates; teachers pair the swan of 1.6 with the two birds of Mundaka 3.1 and Shvetashvatara 4.6–4.7.

o: a crow fed at rites for the ancestors
the eagle that carries the god Vishnu
a swan: the soul that circles the wheel

games.q: who is who in today's verses?
p: tastes sweet and bitter, and grieves

s: the two birds appear in only one Upanishad
they appear in the Mundaka (3.1) and again in the Shvetashvatara (4.6–4.7).
the swan circles because it thinks it and the mover are two
verse 1.6 names that thought as what keeps it wandering.
in verse 1.6 the swan gets free entirely by its own effort
the verse says it reaches the deathless when it is blessed, or favored, by the one who moves the wheel.

games.q: you're the swan, flying circle after circle inside the great wheel. what brings you home, according to the verse?
o: fly faster, until you reach the rim.
stop thinking you and the mover are two, and be met by grace.
leave the wheel and find another one.
games.why: the swan wanders while it thinks it and the mover are separate. favored by that one, it reaches what does not die.

practice: Picture a white bird flying slow circles, each circle one thing you're busy with today, and then let it come down onto still water, wings folding, not even wet.
Let your breath be the water, and whenever a thought lifts you off, let the bird come back down. If you pray, you might rest in the one the verse says turns the wheel.

wordCard.voice: Hamsa, a swan. The Shvetashvatara retells the Mundaka's two birds, and adds the hamsa that circles the wheel until it stops thinking it stands apart.

orig.note: Sanskrit haṃsa: swan or wild goose. in 1.6 the soul that circles the wheel of Brahman.

carryVoice: Your line: the soul wanders while it feels apart from God. Blessed, it comes home. Day four hundred twenty-three, done.

sources.ref: Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.6 (the swan in the wheel of Brahman)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 4.6–4.7 (the two birds on one tree)
